verdict.text:
Track 1 is measurable here, unlike runs where gold labels are empty — there are 31 genuinely-missing slots across the 30 requirements, so the flag rates mean something. But the support is concentrated almost entirely in one slot: condition accounts for 21 of the 31 missing cases, and CoT handles it well (18/21 flagged, precision and recall both 0.86). Every other slot has support of 1–5, so scope (n=1), actor (n=2) and modalVerb (n=2) carry no interpretable signal at all; their f1 values of 0.07, 0.25 and 0.19 are driven by false positives, not by detection failure. The one substantively worrying number is action: 5 gold-missing actions, only 1 flagged, 4 silently filled. That is exactly the fabrication risk the study targets, and 592-Signal shows the mechanism — the source says only "I hate emoji, but this guy requested it", and the model emits `support "emoji"` as a concrete action where two of three humans wrote `<MISSING_ACTION>`. 496-Signal is the same pattern ("it'd be great" → `change the "maximum size of MMS"`). Five cases is far too few to quantify the rate, but the failure mode is consistent enough to name.

The dominant behaviour on this run is the mirror image: CoT over-flags. 26 of 29 implied scopes and 17 of 28 implied modal verbs were marked missing, producing 14 requirements the model called incomplete that the gold called complete, against zero in the other direction. Where humans routinely default to "For all users" and "must", CoT refuses to supply them. That is conservatism, not hallucination, and arguably a safer error — but it makes the overall verdict precision 0.26 and the agreement rate 0.53, and it is what all the low-level metrics are actually measuring.

Similarity sits below the ceiling on every measure: seq_ratio 0.46 vs 0.58 human-human, jaccard 0.28 vs 0.47, cosine 0.60 vs 0.66. The cosine gap is small relative to a std of 0.30 and I would not read much into it; the jaccard gap is the informative one, and it is largely a token-level artifact of the over-flagging — `<MISSING_SCOPE>` and `<MISSING_MODAL_VERB>` where humans wrote real boilerplate. 1504-Signal at 0.02 and 83-Signal at 0.13 are both this.

Paska confirms rather than adds. The two smells map perfectly onto the placeholder behaviour: all 19 failures are "Not requirement", 11 of them also "Incomplete system response / modal verb missing", and every one of the 11 requirements the model judged complete passes (pass_rate 1.0 vs 0.0, a clean split). Paska is detecting the placeholders, not independent quality problems.

The most useful next step is to isolate the scope/modalVerb convention: tell the model explicitly that an unstated audience is "For all users" and an unstated modality is "must", then re-run. That should lift jaccard toward the ceiling and largely empty the Paska failure bucket, and it would leave the action-fabrication question visible on its own rather than buried under placeholder noise. n=30 on the already-atomic subset supports the condition result and the direction of the over-flagging; it does not support any per-slot claim outside condition, nor generalisation to unfiltered requirements.
